sections.overview: MacConnell's bush toad is a little-known toad of the Guiana Highlands. It shares its genus with the pebble toad, O. nigra, but is chiefly associated with moist forest on tepui slopes rather than high rocky summits.
sections.identification: It is a small bufonid, but accessible accounts provide few reliable field marks. It is difficult to detect and partly arboreal; individuals have been found on epiphytic ferns and on the ground.
sections.habitat: It inhabits moist submontane forest with a medium canopy, abundant epiphytes, mosses and dense undergrowth. Records span 800–1800 m in Guyana and Venezuela; presence in neighbouring Brazilian Roraima is possible but unconfirmed. Unlike O. nigra, it is known mainly from forested slopes and foothills.
sections.diet: The sources consulted do not establish its diet.
sections.behavior: It has been observed active at night, usually low on epiphytic ferns, but also on the ground. Its secretive, arboreal habits make it easy to overlook.
sections.reproduction: The breeding site is unknown. Direct development, without a free-living tadpole stage, is presumed for this species but has not been confirmed directly.
sections.ecology: Species-specific prey and ecological interactions remain poorly studied. Although it shares a genus with O. nigra, the two toads are associated with different elevations and habitats.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment published in 2021, based on a 2020 review, classifies it as Vulnerable because its range is restricted to five or fewer threat-defined locations and habitat quality is declining. Mining and fire are potential pressures; distribution and population monitoring are still needed.
